stories.title_en: Forging the Education Commissioner's Letter to Report Lucky Dreams

paragraphs.zh: 庚子年，福建乡科，上府所中诸士，多系沈宗师取在首列者。人皆服沈宗师为得人。
paragraphs.en: In the gengzi year, at the Fujian provincial examination, many of the successful scholars from the upper prefectures were those Education Commissioner Shen had ranked at the top. People all admired Education Commissioner Shen for getting the right men.

paragraphs.zh: 十二月初间，诸举人都上京矣。省城一棍，与本府一善书秀才谋，各诈为沈道一书，用小印图书，护封完密，分递于新春元家。每到一家，则云：“沈爷有书，专差小人来，口嘱付说，你家相公明年必有大捷。他得异梦，特令先来报知，但须谨密勿泄。更某某相公家，与尊府相近，恐他知有专使来，谓老爷厚此薄彼，故亦附有问安书在；特搭带耳，非专为彼来也。”及到他家，所言亦复如是，谓专为此来，餘者都搭带也。及开书看，则字画精楷，书词玄妙，皆称彼得祥梦，其兆应在某，当得大魁。或借其名，或因其地取义，各做一梦语为由，以报他先兆之意。曾见写与举人熊绍祖之书云：“闽省多才，甲于天下，虽京、浙不多让也。特阅麟经诸卷，无如贤最者。以深沉浑厚之养，发以雄俊爽锐之锋，来春大捷南宫，不卜而决矣。子月念二日夜将半，梦一飞熊，手擎红春花，行红日之中，上有金字‘大魁’二字，看甚分明。醒而忆之，日者，建阳也；熊者，君姓也；春花者，君治《春秋》经也。红亦彩色之象，‘大魁’金字则明有吉兆矣。以君之才，叶我之梦，则际明时魁天下，确有明证。若得大魁出于吾门，喜不能寐，人驰报，幸谨之勿泄。”熊举人之家阅之大喜，赏使银三两。请益，复与二两，曰：“明年有大捷，再赏你十两。”及他所奉之书，大抵都述吉梦，都是此意。人赏之者，皆三五金以上。
paragraphs.en: In early the twelfth month, the various juren had already gone up to the capital. A swindler in the provincial city, plotting with a xiucai of this prefecture who was good at calligraphy, each forged a letter from Intendant Shen, using a small seal, wrapping and sealing it tightly, and delivered them separately to the homes of the new provincial graduates. At each house they said: "Master Shen has a letter; he specially sent this humble person. He orally instructed: your young master will surely have a great success next year. He had a strange dream, and specially ordered me to come first and report it, but you must keep it secret and not leak it. Also, such-and-such young master's house is near yours; if he knew a special messenger had come, he would say the master favors one and slights the other, so there is also a greeting letter attached; I just brought it along—I did not come specially for him." When they went to that other house, they said the same, that they had come specially for this one, and the rest were just brought along. When the letters were opened, the handwriting was fine regular script, the wording mysterious and marvelous, all saying he had obtained an auspicious dream, the omen corresponding to so-and-so, who should get the top place. Either borrowing the name, or taking meaning from the place, each made a dream-speech as a pretext, to report the omen in advance. I once saw the letter written to juren Xiong Shaozu: "Fujian has many talents, first in the empire; even the capital and Zhejiang cannot much surpass it. Especially in reading the various scrolls of the Lin classic, none compare with you, sir. With deep, settled, generous cultivation, you send forth a bold, sharp, brilliant edge; next spring's great success at the Southern Palace can be decided without divination. On the twenty-second night of the eleventh month, near midnight, I dreamed of a flying bear, holding a red spring flower, walking in the midst of a red sun, with the gold characters 'Great Champion' above, seen very clearly. On waking I recalled: the sun is Jianyang; the bear is your surname; the spring flower is your study of the Spring and Autumn classic. Red is also an image of color; the gold characters 'Great Champion' clearly have an auspicious omen. With your talent matching my dream, then meeting a bright age and championing the empire has clear proof. If a great champion comes from my school, I cannot sleep for joy; I send a man to report; please keep it secret and do not leak." Xiong the juren's family read it and were overjoyed, rewarded the messenger three taels of silver. He asked for more; they gave two more, saying, "Next year if there is a great success, we'll reward you another ten taels." As for the letters delivered to others, they mostly all told lucky dreams, all this idea. Those who rewarded him all gave three to five taels or more.

paragraphs.zh: 到次年，都银南翮而归，诸春元会时，各述沈道之书叙梦之事，各抚掌大笑曰：“真是好一场春梦也！”此棍真出奇绝巧矣。以此骗人，人谁不乐与之？算其所得，不止百金以上。聊述之以助一笑。
paragraphs.en: The next year they all returned south with clipped wings. When the various new graduates met, each told of Intendant Shen's letter narrating dreams; each clapped and laughed: "Truly a fine spring dream!" This swindler was truly extraordinarily clever. Using this to cheat people—who would not gladly give to him? Counting what he got, it was more than a hundred taels. I briefly record it to add a laugh.

paragraphs.zh: 按：此棍骗新举人，骗亦不痛，虽赏他几两银，亦博得举家人肚中欢喜四个月。惜此棍不再来，若再为之，人亦乐赏之矣。此骗局中最妙者。
paragraphs.en: Note: This swindler cheated new juren, and the cheat did not even hurt much. Though they rewarded him a few taels of silver, they also bought four months of joy in the graduate's household. A pity this swindler did not come again; if he did it again, people would still gladly reward him. This is the finest among swindle schemes.

stories.title_en: Posing as Impermanence and Burning a Writ to Seize People

paragraphs.zh: 长源地方，人烟过千，亦一大市镇也。有一日者，推命人也。至其间推算甚精，断人死生寿夭，最是灵验，以故乡里之老幼男女，多以命与算。凡三年内有该病者、该死者，各问其姓名，暗登记之，以为后验。昼往于市卜命，夜则归宿于僧寺。
paragraphs.en: Changyuan was a place with over a thousand people, also a large market town. There was a day-diviner, a fortune-teller. He came there and calculated very accurately, judging people's death, life, longevity, and early death most effectively, so old and young, men and women of the countryside, many had their fates calculated. Anyone who within three years was due for illness or death, he asked each name and secretly recorded them, for later verification. By day he went to the market to tell fortunes; at night he lodged at a Buddhist monastery.

paragraphs.zh: 有一游方道士至寺，形容半槁，黄瘦黧黑，敬谒日者曰：“闻先生推命极验，敢求此地老幼，有本年命运该死者、当有疾病者，悉以其姓名八字授我，我愿以游方经验药方几种奉换。”日者曰：“你不知命，要此何干？”道士曰：“我自有别用。”日者悉以推过之命，本年有该病者、该死者，尽录付之。道士后乞食诸家，每逢痴愚样人，辄自称是生无常，奉阴司差，同鬼使捕拿此方某人某人等，限此一季到。痴人代之播传，人多未言。又私将黄纸写一牌文，末写“阴司”二大字，中间计开依日者所授之老幼命该死者，写于上半行。又向本僧寺问本地富家男女，及人家钟爱之子姓名，写于后上层。夜间故在社司前，将黄纸牌从下截无人名处焚化，其上半有人名处打灭存之。次日，人来社司祈，见香炉上有黄纸字半截未焚者，取视之，都是乡人姓名，后有“阴司”字，大怪异之，持以传闻于乡。不一月间，此姓名内果死两人，遂相传谓“前瘦道士是生无常，此阴司黄纸牌彼必知之。”凡牌中有名者皆来问，无名者恐下截已焚处有，亦往问之。道士半吞半吐，认是己同鬼使焚的。由是畏死者问：“阴司牌可计免否？”道士曰：“阴司与阳间衙门则同，有银用者，计较免到；或必要再拿者，亦可挨延二三年。奈何不可用银也。”由是，富家男女多以银贿道士，兼以冥财金银，托其计较免到，亦赚得数十金去。其后牌中有名者多不死，反以为得道士计免之力也，岂不惑哉！
paragraphs.en: A wandering Daoist came to the monastery, his appearance half-withered, yellow, thin, and dark. He respectfully visited the day-diviner and said: "I hear you calculate fates extremely accurately. I dare ask for the old and young of this place who this year are fated to die or should have illness; please give me all their names and eight characters. I am willing to exchange several empirically tested wandering-healer prescriptions." The day-diviner said, "You don't know fate-calculation—what do you want this for?" The Daoist said, "I have another use." The day-diviner recorded all the fates he had calculated—those due for illness or death this year—and gave them to him. Afterward the Daoist begged food at various houses; whenever he met someone who looked foolish, he would claim to be Living Impermanence, sent by the underworld, together with ghost-messengers to seize so-and-so and so-and-so of this place, with a deadline of this season. Foolish people spread it for him; many people had not yet spoken of it. He also privately wrote a placard on yellow paper, at the end writing the two large characters "Underworld Office," in the middle listing according to what the day-diviner had given him the old and young fated to die, written on the upper half. He also asked the monastery about the names of sons and daughters of local rich families, and of beloved children, and wrote them on the later upper layer. At night he deliberately went before the earth-god shrine, burned the yellow-paper placard from the lower cut where there were no names, and extinguished the upper half where there were names and kept it. The next day people came to the earth-god shrine to pray, saw on the incense burner a half-burned yellow paper with characters not burned, took it to look: all were names of villagers, with "Underworld Office" after, greatly marveling, and held it to spread through the village. Within a month, two people among these names indeed died, so it was passed around that "the thin Daoist from before is Living Impermanence; this underworld yellow-paper placard he must know about." All whose names were on the placard came to ask; those without names, fearing their names were on the already-burned lower cut, also went to ask. The Daoist half admitted, half withheld, acknowledging that he and the ghost-messengers had burned it. Thus those who feared death asked: "Can the underworld placard be arranged to be excused?" The Daoist said, "The underworld is the same as a yamen in the yang world: those who use silver can arrange to be excused from appearing; or if they must be seized again, it can also be delayed two or three years. How can one not use silver?" Thus men and women of rich families mostly bribed the Daoist with silver, plus paper-money gold and silver for the dead, asking him to arrange to be excused from appearing; he also earned several dozen taels and left. Afterward many of those named on the placard did not die, and they instead thought it was the Daoist's power in arranging the excuse—how deluded!

paragraphs.zh: 按：阴司拘人，何须纸牌？即有牌票，亦何必焚？即焚矣，何为故留残纸餘字以扬于众？此必无之理也。观瘦无常一节，则惑世诬民昭昭矣。人之信鬼幻者，鉴此可以提醒。
paragraphs.en: Note: When the underworld seizes people, why would it need a paper placard? Even if there is a warrant, why must it be burned? Even if burned, why deliberately leave leftover paper and leftover characters to display to the crowd? This is certainly without reason. Looking at the episode of the thin Impermanence, the deluding of the world and deceiving of the people is clear. Those who believe in ghost-illusions can take this as a wake-up.

paragraphs.zh: 城西驿上至建溪陆路一百二十里，常轿价只一钱六分；或路少行客，则减下一钱四分或一钱二分，亦抬。但先邀轿价入手，便五里一放。略有小坡，又放下不抬。大抵坐轿两分，步走一分。凡往来客旅，无不被其笼络者。或当考期，应试士子归家，轿价便增至二钱四分，至少者二钱。不先秤银不抬。若银揽到手，不抬上二十里，便转雇上路夫去，把好价减，只以一分一铺转雇他人抬之。其下手抬者，仍旧五里一放，动曰：“我未得时价。”士子不得已，又重加之。但士人往来简少，都无与较。
paragraphs.en: From Chengxi Station up to Jianxi, the land route is 120 li. The usual chair price is only 1 qian 6 fen; if there are few travelers, they reduce to 1 qian 4 or 1 qian 2, and still carry. But once they get the chair-price in hand first, they set you down every five li. At a slight slope they put you down and don't carry. In general, sitting in the chair is two parts, walking is one part. All traveling guests are caught in this. Or at examination time, when exam candidates go home, the chair price rises to 2 qian 4 fen, at least 2 qian. They won't carry without first weighing out silver. If they get the silver in hand, before carrying twenty li they transfer-hire to upstream bearers, cutting the good price, hiring others to carry at only one fen per stage. Those who then carry still set you down every five li, always saying, "I didn't get the current price." The scholars have no choice but to add more. But scholars travel rarely, and no one argues with them.

paragraphs.zh: 有一提控，不时往来于路，屡被轿夫刁蹬。一日，复要上县，先把两条纸，题四句嘲诗，以方纸包之，再用敝帚柄两个截齐，以绵纸封之，如两匹缎样。次日，自负上路，轿夫争来抬之。提控曰：“吾为一紧急事回家，身无现银。有能送我直到家者，议轿价二钱，又赏汝今晚明早酒饭。若要现银及转雇，则不能也。”内有二轿夫愿抬。遂以两封缎缚于轿，叮咛曰：“善安顿之，勿损坏！”才升轿，又曰：“我到回窑街，要寄一急信与人。你等到那里，慎勿忘也！”未半午后，已到回窑。提控曰：“你在此暂等，我去寄信便来。”其实抽身从小路归家，一饭久不来。两轿夫曰：“他坐话不觉久。有此两匹绸缎在此，我与你奔回，何须等他！”二人疾行，近晚归家。一曰：“各执一匹去。”一曰：“倘有好歹，须相添贴。”两人扯开绵纸，只是两截敝帚柄，重重封裹。又各有一方包，疑是书信。开之，见有纸题大字云：“轿夫常骗人，今也被我骗。若非两帚柄，险失两匹缎。”二人在家大骂曰：“光棍精光棍！”邻家轿夫闻之，入问何故各骂光棍，二轿夫叙其缘由如此。邻轿夫大笑而出，将两帚柄半封半露挂于排栅边，以两纸诗贴于旁。见者诵其诗，又看其帚柄，无不大笑曰：“此提控甚善骗。只你二轿夫亦不合起歹心，早是敝帚柄，故敢扬言骂人；若果是绸缎，你尚恐人知，那相公能寻汝取乎？此是你不是，何骂相公为？”
paragraphs.en: There was a yamen clerk who often traveled this road and was repeatedly given a hard time by chair-bearers. One day he again needed to go up to the county. He first took two strips of paper, wrote four lines of mocking verse, wrapped them in square paper, then took two worn broom handles cut even, sealed them with cotton paper, like two bolts of satin. The next day he carried them on the road himself; chair-bearers competed to carry him. The clerk said, "I have an urgent matter going home and have no ready silver on me. Whoever can take me all the way home, we'll settle the chair price at 2 qian, and I'll also treat you to wine and rice tonight and tomorrow morning. If you want ready silver and transfer-hiring, I cannot." Two chair-bearers among them were willing to carry. He then tied the two sealed "satins" to the chair and instructed: "Settle them well; don't damage them!" Just as he mounted the chair, he added: "When I get to Huiyao Street, I need to send an urgent letter to someone. When you get there, be sure not to forget!" Before half-afternoon they had reached Huiyao. The clerk said, "Wait here a bit; I'll send the letter and come right back." In fact he slipped away by a side path home. After the time of a meal he still hadn't come. The two chair-bearers said, "He's sitting talking and doesn't notice the time. There are these two bolts of silk satin here; let's run back with them—why wait for him!" The two hurried, and near evening reached home. One said, "Each take one bolt." The other said, "If there's good or bad, we'll make up the difference to each other." They tore open the cotton paper: only two cut worn broom handles, wrapped layer upon layer. Each also had a square packet, which they thought was a letter. They opened it and saw paper with large characters: "Chair-bearers often cheat people; now they've been cheated by me too. If not for two broom handles, I'd have nearly lost two bolts of satin." The two cursed loudly at home: "Swindler! Thorough swindler!" Neighboring chair-bearers heard, came in and asked why each was cursing swindler. The two chair-bearers told the story thus. The neighboring chair-bearers laughed loudly and went out, hung the two broom handles half-sealed, half-exposed by the fence-grate, and pasted the two verse-papers beside them. Those who saw recited the verse and looked at the broom handles, all laughing loudly: "This clerk is very good at swindling. Only you two chair-bearers also should not have had ill intent. Luckily they were worn broom handles, so you dare shout and curse people; if they really were silk satin, you'd still fear people knowing—could that gentleman find you and take them back? This is your fault—why curse the gentleman?"

paragraphs.zh: 后三日，提控回，见此诗尚贴在排栅，故问居旁人曰：“前日人寄我两匹缎，被两轿夫抬走，你们亦闻得乎？”人知是此提控弄轿，曰：“你也勿寻缎，那轿夫亦不敢出索轿钱矣。”提控亦大笑而去。
paragraphs.en: Three days later the clerk returned, saw this verse still pasted on the fence-grate, and deliberately asked people living nearby: "The other day someone entrusted me with two bolts of satin; two chair-bearers carried them off—have you heard?" People knew it was this clerk playing with the bearers, and said, "Don't look for the satin; those chair-bearers also dare not come out to demand chair-money." The clerk also laughed loudly and left.

paragraphs.zh: 按：提控骗轿坐者非棍也，此两轿夫则棍耳。不然，何提控再回询问，而轿夫不敢出也？此谓借棍术，还驭棍徒，亦巧矣。然凡远出，若雇轿夫、挑夫，须从店主同雇。彼知役夫根脚，斯无拐逃失落之虞矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: The clerk who swindled a chair-ride was not a swindler; these two chair-bearers were the swindlers. Otherwise, why when the clerk came back to inquire did the chair-bearers dare not come out? This is called borrowing swindler methods to in turn control swindler-fellows—also clever. But whenever traveling far, if hiring chair-bearers or porters, you should hire together with the innkeeper. He knows the laborers' backgrounds; then there is no worry of absconding and loss.

stories.title_en: Fake Purchase at an Alley Gate to Strip Cloth

paragraphs.zh: 建城大街中，旁有一巷，路透后街。巷口为亭，旁列两凳，与人坐息，似人家门下一样。亭旁两边，俱土城，似入人家之门路，稍转，则见前大路矣。
paragraphs.en: In the middle of Jiancheng's main street there is an alley to the side, the road leading through to the back street. At the alley mouth is a pavilion, with two benches beside it for people to sit and rest, like under someone's doorway. On both sides of the pavilion are earthen walls, like the path into someone's house; after a slight turn, you see the front main road.

paragraphs.zh: 忽日，有一棍在亭坐，见客负布而来，认非本城之人，心知其可哄，即叫曰：“买布！客人入亭来。”棍取其布，反复拣择，拿六匹在手，曰：“要买三匹，我拿六匹入内去拣。”即转入巷路，从后大街逃矣。布客在巷凳坐许久，时有一二行路者过此，心疑之，因随其后而入。转一曲墙路，见两旁并无人家，直前则出大路，心方知是被棍脱出。只问街两旁人曰：“方才有一人拿布六匹而来，兄曾见否？”旁人曰：“此巷往来极多，哪知甚人拿布？”布客道其哄买之由，旁人曰：“此是棍明骗去矣。”布客只得大骂，懊恨而去。
paragraphs.en: Suddenly one day a swindler sat in the pavilion, saw a customer coming with cloth on his back, recognized he was not a man of this city, knew he could be fooled, and called: "Buying cloth! Guest, come into the pavilion." The swindler took his cloth, picked back and forth, held six bolts in his hand, and said, "I want to buy three bolts; I'll take six into the inside to pick." He then turned into the alley path and ran off via the back main street. The cloth merchant sat on the alley bench a long time. Then one or two passersby went by; he grew suspicious, so he followed in after them. Turning a winding wall-path, he saw no houses on either side; going straight ahead he came out on the main road; only then did he know he had been stripped by a swindler. He only asked people on both sides of the street: "Just now a man came with six bolts of cloth—did you brothers see him?" Bystanders said, "This alley has extremely many coming and going; how would we know who took cloth?" The cloth merchant told how he had been fooled into a sale. Bystanders said, "This is a swindler who openly cheated it away." The cloth merchant could only curse loudly and leave in regret.

paragraphs.zh: 按：卖物者虽入人门下，亦必跟至其家，见其人居止实落，方可以物付与。不然，虽公共之门，里面人烟丛杂，亦未可轻易信也。商者可以鉴此。
paragraphs.en: Note: When selling goods, even if you enter under someone's door, you must follow to the house, see that the person's dwelling is real and settled, before you can hand over goods. Otherwise, even a public gate, if inside people are crowded and mixed, you still cannot lightly trust. Merchants can take this as a warning.
